# \{brms\} In most cases, we do not have to write our own Stan code, because the {brms} package can do that for us. The `brm()` function in {brms} takes `glm()`-like arguments, and writes accurate and fast Stan code. If `brm()` works for your application, you should much prefer it to writing your own Stan models. It will (probably) be faster and is less likely to have errors. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load packages library(brms) ``` ::: {brms} offers very flexible options for specifying your models and works with {marginaleffects}. We can use it for almost any application, though for simple `lm()` or `glm()` fits, it isn't needed. See `?brms::brm` for the details. There are numerous tutorials available for specific models. ## The `turnout` example Here's the syntax for our usual logistic regression model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load only the turnout data frame and hard-code rescaled variables turnout <- ZeligData::turnout |> mutate(across(age:income, arm::rescale, .names = "rs_{.col}")) # formula f <- vote ~ rs_age + rs_educate + rs_income + race # fit model with glm() fit_glm <- glm(f, data = turnout, family = binomial) # fit model with brm() via cmdstanr fit_brm <- brm(f, data = turnout, family = bernoulli, chains = 10, cores = 10, backend = "cmdstanr") ``` ::: - [CTK: `brm()`'s default backend is still {rstan}; `options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr")` makes {cmdstanr} the default for the session] `glm()` and `brm()` obtain the same estimates.^[The two are not mathematically equal, but they are very close here because {brms}'s default prior on the coefficients is flat. With flat or weak priors and this much data, it is rare that a Bayesian estimate or interval differs from the ML estimate or interval, outside of cases where maximum likelihood fails.] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} library(modelsummary) normalize_terms <- function(x) { x <- sub("^b_", "", x) # brms to glm names x <- ifelse(x == "(Intercept)", "Intercept", x) # unify intercept x } modelsummary( list("glm()" = fit_glm, "brm()" = fit_brm), coef_rename = normalize_terms, statistic = "conf.int", notes = "95% confidence intervals for glm(); 95% credible intervals for brm().", gof_map = NULL ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: {brms} warns only when an R-hat is larger than 1.05, so we check R-hat, ESS, and divergent transitions ourselves. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(posterior) # R-hat and ESS for each parameter summarise_draws(fit_brm, "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 8 × 4 variable rhat ess_bulk ess_tail 1 b_Intercept 1.00 9977. 7302. 2 b_rs_age 1.00 9177. 7265. 3 b_rs_educate 1.00 9036. 6706. 4 b_rs_income 1.00 10362. 7909. 5 b_racewhite 1.00 10487. 7381. 6 Intercept 1.00 9378. 7688. 7 lprior 1.00 9378. 7688. 8 lp__ 1.00 4900. 6602. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # number of divergent transitions after warmup sum(nuts_params(fit_brm, pars = "divergent__")$Value) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: And {brms} plays very nicely with {marginaleffects}. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(marginaleffects) # compute first difference comparisons(fit_brm, variables = list(rs_age = c(-0.5, 0.5)), newdata = datagrid(grid_type = "mean_or_mode")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate 2.5 % 97.5 % 0.167 0.128 0.207 Term: rs_age Type: response Comparison: 0.5 - -0.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # compute and plot expected values (i.e., predicted probabilities) p <- predictions(fit_brm, variables = list(rs_age = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.1)), newdata = datagrid(grid_type = "mean_or_mode")) ggplot(p, aes(x = rs_age, y = estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) + geom_ribbon(fill = "grey") + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03-brms_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The flexibility of MCMC and `brm()` ### Modeling "smooth" relationships To illustrate the power of MCMC and `brm()`, we can imagine fitting a smooth curve for age. The details are not important for now, but this isn't an easy task in our usual framework. But it's straightforward with Bayesian MCMC via `brm()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # smooth relationship between age and voting--notice the s() f <- vote ~ s(rs_age) + rs_educate + rs_income + race smooth_fit <- brm(f, data = turnout, family = bernoulli, chains = 10, cores = 10, backend = "cmdstanr", control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99), # avoids divergent transitions seed = 1234) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # compute and plot expected values (i.e., predicted probabilities) p <- predictions(smooth_fit, variables = list(rs_age = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.1)), newdata = datagrid(grid_type = "mean_or_mode")) ggplot(p, aes(x = rs_age, y = estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) + geom_ribbon(fill = "grey") + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03-brms_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: - [CTK: smooths often cause divergent transitions; with the default `adapt_delta = 0.8` these two fits had 60 and 156 (of 10,000; CmdStan 2.40, `seed = 1234`); `adapt_delta = 0.99` gives none with `seed = 1234` (other seeds occasionally leave 1 of 10,000: 2 of 7 seeds checked)] ### Awkwardly scaled variables Also, `brm()` has no trouble with the variables on their original scales. The original scales pose a serious hurdle for our `metrop()` sampler. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # smooth relationship between age and voting--notice the s() f <- vote ~ s(age) + educate + income + race smooth_fit <- brm(f, data = turnout, family = bernoulli, chains = 10, cores = 10, backend = "cmdstanr", control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99), # avoids divergent transitions seed = 1234) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # compute and plot expected values (i.e., predicted probabilities) p <- predictions(smooth_fit, variables = list(age = seq(18, 90, by = 1)), newdata = datagrid(grid_type = "mean_or_mode")) ggplot(p, aes(x = age, y = estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) + geom_ribbon(fill = "grey") + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03-brms_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
